Amandeep: The Pune offer closes Friday. We're going. I've explained all the reasons.
Salma: I know the reasons. I just need more time to think about my team here
Amandeep: How many times do I have to say it? After everything I've done for us, this is the least you can do.
Salma: That's not fair
Amandeep: Then tell me what's fair. I'm the one carrying us.
Salma: Fine. I'll tell them Monday.
Four months later.
Salma: Why did you leave the plates again??
Amandeep: It's plates. Calm down
Salma: It's not the plates. You never asked me about Pune, you told me. I've been angry since then.
Amandeep: That was months ago!
Salma: Not for me.

qa.q: What does Salma's line "It's not the plates" suggest about how Salma feels?

qa.q: What could Amandeep have done differently at the start?
qa.a: Amandeep could have listened to Salma's worry about the team and looked at options together instead of repeating reasons and using guilt, so the decision would have been shared.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see the argument about the plates?
qa.a: Amandeep may feel confused and defensive, since the move seems long past, without seeing that the anger from Pune never went away.

grounding: One partner presses with repeated reasons and guilt, the other gives in, and the resentment resurfaces months later in an unrelated fight.

In the small town of Bolpur, Anirban had been offered a teaching post in Kolkata, and Payal did not want to leave her mother or her sewing unit.
Every evening, Anirban brought it up again. The same reasons, louder each time. "Think of our future. Think of the children we'll have. Do you want them to grow up in a small town because you're scared?" Once he said, "My father always said a wife's place is beside her husband. Maybe he was right."
After two weeks, Payal said quietly, "Fine. We'll go."
They moved in June. Anirban was happy with his job. Payal found a small flat to work from, but she missed her mother and her workers.
Eight months later, when Anirban forgot to buy vegetables, Payal suddenly shouted, "You never think about what I gave up!" He stared at her, confused. It was about vegetables, wasn't it?

qa.q: Where had Anirban been offered a teaching post?
What was Payal feeling when she suddenly shouted about the vegetables?
qa.a: Payal was full of resentment that had built up since she gave in under guilt and pressure, and it burst out over a small thing.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Anirban handled the offer?
qa.a: Instead of repeating reasons more forcefully and using guilt, he could listen to what Payal would lose and look for options together, like a trial period.

qa.q: How is Anirban affected months later?
qa.a: Anirban is confused and caught off guard, not realising the argument he 'won' left resentment that now shows up in unrelated fights.

grounding: It shows a partner winning a move through pressure and guilt while the other gives in, and resentment returning months later in an unrelated fight.

Daniel had been offered a job in Vancouver, and he wanted it badly. Nour loved her lab in Montreal.
He didn't shout. He just kept talking. At breakfast, in the car, before bed. "This is a once-in-ten-years chance." "Your lab will always be there." "I supported you through your PhD, didn't I?" Each time, a little more pointed.
After three weeks Nour said, "Okay. Let's go." She didn't feel convinced. She felt tired.
They moved in September. Daniel thrived. Nour found a lab, but a smaller one, and the work felt like starting over.
In February, Daniel forgot to call when he was going to be late. Nour exploded. "Of course. Your schedule. Your job. Your city. Everything is yours." Daniel stood in the hallway with his coat still on, stunned.
The fight wasn't about a phone call. It was about three weeks in a kitchen in Montreal.

qa.q: Where had Daniel been offered a job?
How did Nour feel when she agreed to move?
qa.a: Nour felt tired and worn down rather than convinced, giving in after weeks of pressure.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Daniel and Nour better than pushing until one gives in?
qa.a: They could each write what matters most and look at options together, such as a trial arrangement, so neither decision comes from pressure.

qa.q: How does the move look to Daniel months later?
qa.a: Daniel is stunned by Nour's outburst, not realising the pressure he used left resentment that now appears in unrelated fights.

grounding: It shows a partner pressing reasons and guilt until the other gives in, with resentment reappearing months later in an unrelated fight.
